purpose: Make a Spark available through your NVIDIA Brev account.
steps: Open the NVIDIA instructions and log in to your own Brev account. / Select the device registration flow and review who will receive access. / Register one device, configure its SSH access in Brev, and check the device page. / Try access with the intended account before registering another device.
success: Brev shows the correct device as healthy and the intended user can connect.
attention: Registration adds another remote-access path. Keep registration keys out of notes, chat and command history. Deregister in Brev to undo it; do not replace SparkBox's saved trust.

purpose: Use a local model to help write code from a terminal.
steps: Choose the Claude Code, OpenCode or Codex instructions; follow only that path. / In Ollama, download the Qwen model that fits the node and test a short question. / Install the chosen agent in a project you can restore, then connect it to Ollama. / Ask it to change one small file, inspect the change, and run the project's checks.
success: The agent answers using the intended local model and a small coding task passes its checks.
attention: Agent tools can edit files and run programs. Choose access to a specific project; optional messaging and external services require their own decisions. Installing Ollama or the agent is a manual step.

purpose: Build image and video workflows in a browser with ComfyUI.
steps: Start with Image Gen Quick Start and its smaller Z-Image-Turbo model. / Check free disk space, create the named Python environment, and follow the matching PyTorch installation. / Download each model into the folder named in the guide, then start ComfyUI and reach port 8188 through a deliberate connection. / Load the supplied workflow, generate one image, and save it before trying the larger video path.
success: ComfyUI opens, finds the chosen weights, and produces a saved image or video without missing-node errors.
attention: Image and video paths use different environments. Video needs much more memory and storage. Stop other GPU work through its owning app first. Keep generated outputs before removing an environment.

purpose: Choose and verify the physical layout for two to four Sparks.
steps: Open Topology and Fabric to record your current cables, port names and addresses. / Choose the diagram for the number of Sparks you own and connect the cables accordingly. / Use the guide's NVIDIA Sync path or its manual dry run only for a new, deliberately planned network. / Compare the resulting interfaces and links in Fabric, then test a small distributed workload separately.
success: Each intended link has the expected speed and each device retains its management connection.
attention: Your existing four-node switch uses all four physical 200 Gb/s sockets. Example addresses are not instructions to replace its working configuration. Network changes need a recovery path at each device.

purpose: Understand and set up a three-Spark ring.
steps: Compare the ring diagram with your physical equipment before making changes. / Record each node's two fabric interfaces and management address. / Follow the manual addressing and inter-device SSH steps only on the intended three-node layout. / Check all three paths in Fabric before attempting NCCL.
success: All three ring links communicate, while management access stays available.
attention: This is a different layout from the owner's four-port switch. Applying ring netplan examples to the existing switch fabric can disconnect nodes. Keep the original network files for rollback.

purpose: Reach a Spark from your computer and open its remote applications.
steps: In SparkBox, use Connect to find or add the node and verify its identity. / Open Terminal for a remote command line or RDP for desktop checks. / If you also want NVIDIA Sync, follow its separate install and device onboarding path. / Open one remote application and confirm it belongs to the intended node.
success: The expected node connects and its application can be reached through the chosen connection.
attention: NVIDIA Sync and Tailscale are optional, separate products. SparkBox's built-in VPN is already configured; this guide does not authorize changing it or copying another app's SSH trust.

purpose: Connect two Sparks directly for distributed work.
steps: Record the management addresses and fabric interfaces in SparkBox. / Cable the two devices using the direct-link diagram. / Review the guide's addressing and SSH setup against those actual interfaces. / Check the link and communication in Fabric before starting a two-node load.
success: Both management connections remain available and the direct fabric link works at its expected speed.
attention: Direct-link instructions do not describe the owner's four-node switch. Save existing network settings before a deliberate reconfiguration; do not reuse example IP addresses blindly.

purpose: Understand the two-Station ConnectX-8 setup.
steps: Confirm both machines are DGX Stations with the specified CX8 adapters. / Read the control-host setup and probe steps before cabling the two rails. / Review the per-rail addresses and run the guide's prerequisite checks. / Validate the core links before considering optional GPU-direct or boot-parameter changes.
success: Both Station rails meet the guide's link and communication checks.
attention: This targets 400 Gb/s CX8 Station hardware, not the GB10/CX7 Spark cluster. SparkBox offers this as reference only; no Spark action applies these settings.

purpose: Run familiar data-analysis tools on the Spark GPU.
steps: Confirm the guide's CUDA and Python versions, then create its dedicated RAPIDS environment. / Clone the matching notebook assets and start JupyterLab. / Select the environment's notebook kernel and run the introductory cells in order. / Compare GPU output with the CPU example and save the notebook and results.
success: The notebook finishes with matching results and reports GPU-backed operations.
attention: Use the guide's matching RAPIDS, Python and CUDA versions together. Creating a separate environment avoids replacing system Python; record its name so it can be removed later.

purpose: Spread NumPy-style array calculations across Spark GPUs.
steps: Begin with the single-node cuPyNumeric example and verify its output. / For several nodes, record the intended fabric and shared-data paths first. / Review the guide's MPI, shared-storage and environment setup for every participating node. / Run a small distributed calculation and compare the answer before scaling the data.
success: The small calculation gives the expected answer on one node and on the chosen cluster layout.
attention: Shared storage, firewall and MPI setup can change the host network. SparkBox does not apply these examples automatically. Verify permissions and restore points before the multi-node path.

purpose: Measure GPU kernels and learn how cuTile speeds up calculations.
steps: Prepare the listed CUDA development image, then clone the pinned TileGym version. / Run one kernel benchmark and read its timing output before the full suite. / For model inference, obtain the selected model and compare the ordinary PyTorch result with the cuTile result. / Save the commands, model settings and timings together for a repeatable comparison.
success: Correctness checks pass and timing reports identify the exact kernel or model measured.
attention: Container preparation only downloads the image. Building kernels and running benchmarks consume GPU time; first compilation can be slow. Do not treat performance numbers from another GPU as Spark guarantees.

purpose: Open DGX Dashboard, use JupyterLab and watch GPU activity.
steps: Use the node's application access to reach its DGX Dashboard on port 11000. / Log in with the node's own account, then start a JupyterLab instance. / Run the sample notebook and watch resource use in SparkBox's Dashboard. / Save the notebook and stop JupyterLab when finished; use SparkBox Updates for package maintenance.
success: JupyterLab reaches Running and the sample produces an output you can save.
attention: The original NVIDIA text includes system and firmware updates with an automatic restart. Use SparkBox Updates and its separate restart/health checks for this cluster. Do not bypass an outstanding protected-update checkpoint.

purpose: Read the Station-specific agent skills and qualified model workflow.
steps: Confirm the device is the supported GB300 Station. / Preview the installer against a chosen project before installing its four skills. / Inspect the detected release profile and the one qualified inference recipe. / Use explicit confirmation for launch and verify the labelled service before cleanup.
success: The Station tool reports its hardware profile and the qualified recipe's checks pass.
attention: These skills are for DGX Station, not DGX Spark. Their installer and MIG actions are not run by SparkBox. Keep ownership boundaries between its services and SparkBox services.

purpose: Learn which fine-tuning method fits a task and a GPU.
steps: Read the differences between LoRA, QLoRA and full fine-tuning. / Choose a small dataset with examples of the result you want. / Compare the model and training method with your actual memory budget. / For a Spark hands-on walkthrough, open the separate Unsloth or PyTorch playbook.
success: You have chosen a method, model and evaluation set before starting a training job.
attention: This overview's hardware table targets GeForce RTX and RTX PRO. It is reference material, not a validated Spark installation recipe. Training quality needs evaluation on examples held out of training.

purpose: Teach FLUX.2 Klein a character, object or style with a small adapter.
steps: Select the 4B or 9B path according to the node's memory and obtain model access. / Prepare the AI Toolkit environment and generate a base image before training. / Put your labelled example images in the specified dataset folders and review training settings. / Train the adapter, then load it in ComfyUI and compare matching prompts against the base model.
success: The saved LoRA loads and produces a visible, repeatable difference for the intended concept.
attention: Keep the dataset and trained adapter outside disposable containers. Image rights and model access are owner decisions. A four-hour estimate does not guarantee training completion on every configuration.

purpose: Read how to adapt Isaac GR00T to robot demonstrations.
steps: Confirm the specified DGX Station and disk budget. / Use the n1.6-release branch and its matching datasets. / Check the video decoder and apply the documented PyAV workaround only when needed. / Verify base inference, train a short run, and evaluate it before using any robot.
success: The reference evaluation completes with a saved checkpoint and interpretable action output.
attention: This current guide targets GB300 Station memory. Its optional dependency script can install CUDA system packages. It is reference only for the Spark cluster; a model result is not authorization for physical robot motion.

purpose: Explore a local, isolated healthcare-agent software example.
steps: Confirm the Station's memory and storage meet the guide. / Start with the supplied example data and configure its local model services. / Deploy the OpenShell environment and check its network isolation. / Run the example queries and inspect the source records behind each generated answer.
success: The example dashboard responds and its isolation checks match the intended policy.
attention: This is a Station-only software demonstration with a large memory requirement. Keep real patient data out of initial tests. Generated summaries require qualified review and do not establish clinical accuracy.

purpose: Connect Hermes to a local vLLM model.
steps: Use Models to prepare and load a compatible coding model, then check its endpoint. / Follow the Hermes installation path in a project you can restore. / Configure Hermes to use that specific endpoint and start a short terminal conversation. / Review enabled tools and test one small project task before adding optional messaging.
success: Hermes responds through the intended local endpoint and its test task has an inspectable result.
attention: Tool access and Telegram are separate permissions. Keep model credentials in the destination application's secure settings; do not paste them into How To notes or AI prompts.

purpose: Build Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab for simulated robot training.
steps: Check available disk space and the compiler prerequisites. / Clone the exact Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab revisions listed together in the guide. / Build Sim, connect Lab to that installation, and launch the small example. / Save the training output and verify the example completes before changing environments.
success: Isaac Sim opens and the named Lab reinforcement-learning example runs.
attention: This source build is substantial and needs matching Sim/Lab versions. Installing compilers changes packages; review that separately. A simulation result does not prove a real robot is ready.

purpose: Compare NumPy calculations with GPU-accelerated JAX.
steps: Clone the JAX playbook assets and build their local container image. / Start the notebook service with the guide's port mapping and open marimo. / Run the NumPy baseline, then each JAX variant on the same data. / Check equal results and record compilation time separately from repeated execution time.
success: The notebook produces matching calculations and comparable timing measurements.
attention: The local jax-playbook image must be built from assets, not pulled as a registry tag. Notebook access must be deliberate; stop the container after saving your work.

purpose: Learn to profile and optimize training with Triton kernels.
steps: Confirm the guide's GB300 Station and storage prerequisites. / Profile the baseline Llama fine-tuning step and identify its slow operations. / Implement and test RMSNorm before the cross-entropy kernel. / Compare correctness, memory use and full training time with the unchanged baseline.
success: Correctness tests pass and the profile shows the measured effect of each kernel.
attention: This guide targets DGX Station and an explicitly selected GPU. The Spark library retains it as reference; its reported performance is not a Spark acceptance result.

purpose: Ask a vision model about live webcam images.
steps: Install the selected Ollama vision model and check that it can read one still image. / Install Live VLM WebUI in its separate environment and start its HTTPS service. / Open the page, approve only the intended camera, and select the local model endpoint. / Begin with a low frame rate and verify that responses describe the visible scene.
success: The page displays new frames, relevant model answers and measured response times.
attention: WebRTC needs direct connectivity and the browser's camera permission. A SparkBox tunnel alone does not prove media connectivity. A cloud backend would send camera frames outside the node.

purpose: Read how to connect a local AI workspace to Home Assistant.
steps: Confirm the Windows ARM64 platform in the guide. / Start with a lamp you can watch and select only that device. / Review a proposed action, apply it, and verify the lamp's actual state. / Test an automation once before choosing any recurring jobs.
success: The selected device behaves as approved and the saved report can be reopened.
attention: This targets RTX Spark on Windows, not DGX OS. Saved automations can outlive the browser. Device control and household credentials are not automated by SparkBox.

purpose: Build llama.cpp and serve a GGUF model from a Spark.
steps: Check the build tools, free disk and model memory requirement. / Follow the CUDA build instructions for Spark's architecture. / Start the selected GGUF model with a deliberate listen address and port. / Test the local API, then add the endpoint in Providers and try a short Chat request.
success: The API lists the intended model and a short answer completes through SparkBox Chat.
attention: llama.cpp installation and launch remain manual. It is not a SparkBox-owned vLLM load, so stop it with its own documented controls. Keep the model cache when removing build artifacts unless you intend to delete it.

purpose: Fine-tune a model using LLaMA Factory's training configurations.
steps: Create the separate Python environment and verify PyTorch can see CUDA. / Install the matching LLaMA Factory revision and inspect the example dataset. / Start with the smallest suitable LoRA configuration and save checkpoints outside temporary folders. / Run inference with the result and compare it with the base model before export.
success: Training produces a readable checkpoint and the exported model answers the evaluation examples.
attention: Full training uses more memory than LoRA. Keep sequence length and batch size within the node's memory, and evaluate on unseen examples. Package installation is not run automatically.

purpose: Choose a local model and a way to use it for chat, coding or documents.
steps: Decide whether you need chat, a coding agent or document questions. / Choose a model that leaves memory for the operating system and your expected conversation length. / Use Models or the appropriate engine guide to start it, then test a short question. / Connect the chosen app to the verified local endpoint and check its data-sharing settings.
success: The intended app answers using the model and endpoint you selected.
attention: This is an overview, not a version-pinned installation recipe. Model size alone does not determine memory use; context and simultaneous requests matter too.

purpose: Run LM Studio's headless server and reach it from a laptop.
steps: Confirm the example model fits the 128 GB Spark and available disk. / Install llmster and start the LM Studio API service. / Download and load the chosen model, then test the node's local endpoint. / Add that endpoint to Providers or connect the laptop SDK; use LM Link only if you choose its separate pairing flow.
success: The model is loaded and a request to the selected endpoint returns a complete answer.
attention: The guide's large example is not a 64 GB default. LM Studio owns this service; SparkBox can use its endpoint but does not claim ownership of its lifecycle.

purpose: Read the Station-specific Claude Code and Ollama walkthrough.
steps: Confirm the guide's Station environment. / Install the compatible Ollama version and test the named coding model. / Connect Claude Code through the documented local-provider path. / Use a disposable project for the first edit and inspect every changed file.
success: The coding agent answers through the local model and the test project's checks pass.
attention: The current guide targets DGX Station. Use CLI Coding Agents with Local Inference for the Spark-specific path. Agent access to files and commands needs deliberate limits.

purpose: Understand GPU partitioning on DGX Station.
steps: Read the B300 prerequisites and inspect the supported profiles. / Stop affected work through its owning application before a planned layout change. / Follow the Station-specific enable, layout and verification steps. / Test an explicitly selected instance and use the documented restore procedure when finished.
success: The intended Station GPU instances appear and a test workload uses the chosen instance.
attention: GB10 Sparks do not use this B300 MIG procedure. It can reset GPU availability and remove instances; no SparkBox automation is offered.

purpose: Build a local chatbot with several specialist agents and document retrieval.
steps: Reserve the memory and disk stated for the default model set. / Clone the project, review its configuration and obtain the model access it needs. / Start the documented Compose stack and wait for every backend to become ready. / Open the frontend and try the supplied sample prompts, checking which agent handled each.
success: The frontend responds, routes requests, and retrieves the intended documents.
attention: The default stack approaches a 128 GB Spark's memory limit. Do not run it beside another heavy load. It uses services outside SparkBox's ownership; preserve documents and data volumes during cleanup.

purpose: Understand a PC with two matching discrete GPUs.
steps: Check the guide's requirement for matching GPUs and the motherboard's lane layout. / Choose the llama.cpp or ComfyUI section for the application you use. / Run one small example and verify both GPUs participate. / Compare output and timing before increasing model size or resolution.
success: The chosen PC application uses both intended GPUs and produces a correct output.
attention: This describes GPUs inside a PC, not separate DGX Spark nodes. Do not apply PC power, PCIe or tensor-split assumptions to the Spark fabric.

purpose: Run and compare optimized FLUX image generation with TensorRT.
steps: Prepare the listed PyTorch image and check the free-memory requirement. / Clone the matching TensorRT examples and install their dependencies inside the container. / Generate an image with the baseline precision, then repeat with the selected optimized precision. / Compare image quality, runtime and saved output before using a quantized version.
success: Both paths produce images and their measured quality and speed can be compared.
attention: Compilation and quantization can need extra memory. The image download does not compile or launch the workload. Keep output files in a persistent directory.

purpose: Understand the switch fabric linking four or more Sparks.
steps: Open Topology and confirm the actual switch model and occupied sockets. / Record each node-to-port cable and negotiated speed in Fabric. / Compare the guide's addressing with your saved inventory before considering a change. / Validate communication on every intended path, then test distributed compute separately.
success: All intended nodes have working fabric links and retain management access.
attention: The owner's MikroTik has four physical 200 Gb/s QSFP56 ports, all occupied. Upstream generic port examples are not a hardware inventory. Switch, bridge and netplan edits remain manual and require recovery access.

purpose: Read the Station walkthrough for training a small chat model from scratch.
steps: Confirm the Station's storage and memory budget. / Prepare the documented dataset and container environment. / Run a short pipeline through tokenization, pretraining and chat fine-tuning. / Read the report and compare saved checkpoints in the provided chat interface.
success: The full sample pipeline produces a report and a checkpoint that can answer a chat prompt.
attention: This is Station-only and a full run can take many hours. Tracking services and dataset accounts are separate choices. Preserve checkpoints before removing containers.

purpose: Check that GPUs can communicate across the Spark fabric.
steps: Use Fabric to check links and verify that each node is the intended trusted device. / Follow the two-, three- or four-node section matching your layout. / Build the pinned NCCL and test suite for Spark's architecture on the participating nodes. / Run the small all-reduce test, save its output and compare all nodes before increasing message sizes.
success: The test completes without communication errors and reports bandwidth for the actual topology.
attention: SparkBox's fabric checks are prerequisites, not an NCCL benchmark. Building and running the upstream test remains manual; do not let example hostfiles overwrite your known addresses.

purpose: Adapt a model with NeMo AutoModel.
steps: Prepare the listed NeMo image and matching pinned source revision. / Choose a small example that fits the node and obtain its model and dataset access. / Review the training configuration and run a short fine-tune. / Verify the saved checkpoint on held-out examples before an optional export or publication.
success: Training completes and a saved checkpoint loads for evaluation.
attention: Publishing to Hugging Face is a separate explicit action. Keep tokens out of this library and use protected authentication in the destination tool. Multi-node training is beyond the guide's single-node example.

purpose: Run an agent inside NemoClaw's controlled environment.
steps: Prepare a compatible local inference endpoint and read the installer changes. / Follow onboarding for the Spark path and review every allowed network destination. / Open the agent UI and try a small task using only an intended project. / Check its behavior and stop services through NemoClaw when finished.
success: The agent answers through the chosen model and its allowed access matches your settings.
attention: Express install can download large models and install services. The two-node Station section is not a Spark recipe; the linked two-Spark path is experimental. Messaging and public tunnels need separate approval.

purpose: Try practical tasks with an already configured NemoClaw agent.
steps: Finish and test the companion NemoClaw setup first. / Pick one application tab and read its required sources, project access and network policy. / Run the supplied prompt once and inspect the result. / Personalize the task only after that test; enable recurring work or Telegram only when you intend it.
success: The selected example produces an inspectable report or project result using the allowed resources.
attention: This long guide contains several independent examples. Work on one tab at a time. Recurring jobs, Telegram and cloudflared are optional external actions, not automatic SparkBox steps.

purpose: Choose and serve a Nemotron model on a Spark.
steps: Choose Nano or Super and read the memory and engine requirements for that path. / Prepare the matching reviewed image and model files. / Use Models for a compatible vLLM load, reviewing parser and memory settings before starting. / Test the endpoint and a short Chat request, then record the exact model and image used.
success: The server lists the intended Nemotron model and returns a complete answer with the expected parser behavior.
attention: Nano and Super use different images and settings. Parser code and remote-code permissions need review; a downloaded image alone does not prove model compatibility. TensorRT-LLM launch remains manual.

purpose: Expose a model through an NVIDIA NIM container.
steps: Choose the NIM model and precision that fit the node. / Obtain the required NGC access using its protected login flow. / Follow the selected container's cache, address and port settings. / Wait for readiness, test the API, and add its endpoint in Providers for Chat.
success: The NIM endpoint becomes ready and answers a request for the intended model.
attention: NGC authentication, model licenses and registry access are owner decisions. This guide's latest tag can change. SparkBox does not run an arbitrary NIM container or store its login key in notes.

purpose: Read how to compare NVFP4 and BF16 pretraining on Station.
steps: Confirm the GB300 Station and the specified NeMo container. / Read the training script before starting the short mock-data run. / Repeat with BF16 using the same settings. / Compare speed and memory, then prepare a real dataset only after the short pipeline works.
success: Both sample runs finish and record comparable measurements.
attention: This targets Station, and mock data does not establish training quality. SparkBox does not offer a Spark launch action for this recipe.

purpose: Make a smaller NVFP4 checkpoint and evaluate it.
steps: Choose the Spark platform settings and obtain the source model's access. / Prepare the matching container and a separate output directory. / Run the Model Optimizer quantization and watch disk and memory use. / Verify all output files, serve the result with a compatible engine, and compare evaluation answers with the base model.
success: The saved quantized checkpoint loads and its quality is acceptable on your own evaluation set.
attention: Quantization can change answers. Preserve the original model and keep output separate. Station launch variables and GPU indexes must not be copied to Spark unchanged.

purpose: Chat in a browser using Open WebUI and Ollama.
steps: Prepare the reviewed Open WebUI image and choose desktop or NVIDIA Sync access. / Start the guide's container with deliberate ports and persistent storage. / Create the first administrator account and download a model that fits the node. / Send a short question, save a conversation, then stop the service using the same path that started it.
success: The browser shows a complete answer and retains the conversation after a controlled restart.
attention: Image preparation does not start the container or create its account. Keep persistent volumes when stopping it. Do not expose an unfinished first-run administrator screen to an untrusted network.

purpose: Connect OpenClaw to a local model.
steps: Review the installer and choose the Linux path for a DGX Spark. / Prepare a compatible local model in Models and verify its endpoint. / Complete OpenClaw onboarding with that provider and only the tools you intend to allow. / Test a small task in the web UI before adding channels or extra skills.
success: The agent responds through the selected local model with the intended tool access.
attention: An agent can run commands and access files through its tools. A local model alone does not isolate those tools. Consider the separate OpenShell guide before giving broad access.

purpose: Limit an AI agent's files, network access and processes with OpenShell.
steps: Prepare and test a local vLLM endpoint in SparkBox. / Review the OpenShell installation and build the guide's Pi agent image. / Create the provider profile and allow only the destinations needed for the task. / Start the sandbox, run the isolation checks, and try a small task in a selected project.
success: The agent reaches its allowed model while the documented forbidden accesses are denied.
attention: The installer and policy edits remain manual. Keep existing Docker settings and services in mind; do not replace a daemon configuration wholesale. Passing one example does not prove all future tools are isolated.

purpose: Route independent requests among trusted systems with NVIDIA PAIR.
steps: Install the package matching each system's OS and architecture. / Start an engine and verify its model locally on each serving system. / Pair only systems you recognize, then copy the local endpoint into the intended client. / Send a test request and inspect PAIR's routing activity.
success: Requests reach an available system with the requested model and routing activity identifies it.
attention: PAIR routes requests; it does not split one model across Spark GPUs. Pairing and trust are separate from SparkBox's own identity checks. Remove peers in PAIR to undo pairing.

purpose: Run a sample portfolio calculation with GPU-accelerated cuOpt.
steps: Prepare the RAPIDS notebook image and confirm the stated free memory. / Open the supplied notebook with its sample data. / Run each cell and inspect the solver's completion status and constraints. / Save the notebook and compare its timing and results with the provided baseline.
success: The sample optimization completes and its visualizations and solver status can be inspected.
attention: This is a software and mathematical example, not an investment recommendation. Changed data or constraints need their own validation. Save results before stopping the notebook container.

purpose: Fine-tune a model with PyTorch using full training, LoRA or QLoRA.
steps: Prepare the listed PyTorch image and start with the single-node section. / Obtain model access, select a small example and read its memory settings. / Run a short training job and save the checkpoint in a persistent folder. / Evaluate it before considering the separate two-node instructions.
success: A short training run finishes and its checkpoint can be loaded for evaluation.
attention: The distributed path changes Docker configuration and creates a Swarm. SparkBox does not apply those changes automatically. Preserve existing services and use the path's rollback instructions only for resources it created.

purpose: Ask questions of documents with an AI Workbench RAG example.
steps: Install and open AI Workbench on the intended device. / Clone the named agentic-RAG project and read its provider requirements. / Put API credentials in Workbench's own secret fields, then launch the chat app. / Ask a question about a supplied document and inspect the retrieved evidence.
success: The app answers and shows relevant document evidence for the test question.
attention: The example uses external model APIs. Document text may be sent to those services and usage may have costs. Start with sample documents and choose providers deliberately.

purpose: Serve a model with SGLang and test structured answers.
steps: Choose a model and container supported for the Spark's memory. / Use Models to review a compatible SGLang load, including context, port and parser settings. / Start the load through its normal confirmation and wait for the endpoint to become ready. / Test a short Chat request, then follow the source examples for repeated-prefix chat and JSON output.
success: The endpoint answers and the structured-output test returns the requested valid shape.
attention: Prefix-cache speed must be judged with matching settings and logs, not one elapsed time. The current guide includes Station choices too; select the Spark path.

purpose: Read the Station-specific SGLang inference and benchmark procedure.
steps: Confirm the Station's GB300 GPU and select its index explicitly. / Prepare the guide's container and start the default small model. / Test ordinary chat and structured output before the parallel benchmark. / Read cache statistics together with timing results.
success: The selected Station GPU serves the model and the output tests pass.
attention: This reference targets DGX Station. Use Serve LLMs with SGLang for Spark settings; do not apply Station-specific GPU selection or memory budgets to GB10.

purpose: Analyze sample single-cell RNA data with GPU notebooks.
steps: Prepare the RAPIDS notebook image and check free disk and memory. / Open the supplied notebook and load its sample dataset. / Run quality checks, filtering, dimensionality reduction and clustering in order. / Save the notebook, plots and processed data before stopping the container.
success: The sample pipeline completes and its quality-control plots and clusters can be inspected.
attention: The guide demonstrates a data-processing workflow, not biological or clinical validity for new data. Larger datasets need a fresh memory budget and domain review.

purpose: Run an interactive photo booth with a Reachy Mini robot.
steps: Confirm the required robot, display, audio and local desktop are available. / Follow the project setup and obtain the listed models' access. / Test the robot's camera and audio before starting the full stack. / Generate one photo, check where it is stored, and stop the stack before unplugging devices.
success: The robot interaction, photo capture and generated image all complete in the local UI.
attention: Physical hardware and USB permissions are required. Optional QR sharing makes photos reachable on the network. SparkBox does not move the robot, publish photos or update its firmware automatically.

purpose: Compare ordinary inference with a faster draft-and-verify method.
steps: Prepare the listed TensorRT-LLM image and choose a compatible model pair or method. / Start with the single-node example and a small context. / Send matching prompts and measure answer quality and token speed. / Attempt the separate distributed instructions only after the fabric and single-node run are verified.
success: The API responds and a controlled comparison shows whether speculation helps this workload.
attention: Image preparation does not launch TensorRT-LLM. Distributed MPI and container entrypoints require review. Keep model caches when stopping a test unless you deliberately want to remove them.

purpose: Read an optional Tailscale remote-access setup.
steps: Decide whether you need a second remote-access system alongside SparkBox's VPN. / If you choose it, review its account, routing and SSH settings before installing. / Join one node and one client, then test from the intended network. / Confirm SparkBox connectivity still works before adding more devices.
success: The intended client can reach the selected node and the existing connection still works.
attention: The built-in VPN already works. This guide does not change it or enable Tailscale automatically. Keep a local recovery path and remove the optional service through its own cleanup steps.

purpose: Understand NVIDIA's playbook publishing template.
steps: Read the example metadata and page layout. / Copy the template only into a separate documentation project. / Replace its example text and check the publishing format. / Review the result as documentation rather than a Spark workload.
success: A sample documentation page has the expected tabs and metadata.
attention: This is a publishing example, not an installation or compute workflow. It has no node automation.

purpose: Understand the Station playbook publishing template.
steps: Read the example metadata and page layout. / Copy the template only into a separate documentation project. / Replace its example text and check the publishing format. / Review the result as documentation rather than a Station workload.
success: A sample documentation page has the expected tabs and metadata.
attention: This is a publishing example, not an installation or compute workflow. It has no node automation.

purpose: Read a Station notebook for finding topics in a large text collection.
steps: Confirm the Station memory and the matching RAPIDS environment. / Download the sample dataset and notebook assets. / Run embeddings, clustering and the topic visualizations in order. / Save the results and inspect representative documents for each topic.
success: The notebook finishes and representative examples support the topic labels.
attention: The current guide targets DGX Station and a large dataset. Its storage and performance numbers are not Spark guarantees. Treat model-generated topic labels as results to inspect.

purpose: Serve and test models with TensorRT-LLM.
steps: Select the single-node section and its exact image before preparing the environment. / Validate the engine with the guide's small example. / Start the API server with a deliberate port and model settings, then add the verified endpoint in Providers. / Test Chat before following the optional Open WebUI or distributed sections.
success: The chosen model answers through its API and the configured client.
attention: Single-node and distributed sections use different image tags. TensorRT-LLM launch and MPI setup remain manual; SparkBox's Models lifecycle does not own those containers.

purpose: Turn sample documents into a searchable knowledge graph.
steps: Choose the intended local model and verify its endpoint. / Clone the txt2kg project and start its documented services. / Upload a small non-sensitive document and inspect the extracted entities and relationships. / Compare the graph with the source before processing a larger collection.
success: The graph can be queried and its relationships can be traced to the uploaded document.
attention: Extraction can invent or miss relationships. Preserve graph storage when stopping containers. External model endpoints may receive document contents; choose them deliberately.

purpose: Run a memory-efficient fine-tuning example with Unsloth.
steps: Prepare the listed PyTorch image and read the matching dependency versions. / Install Unsloth inside the container and obtain the validation script from the pinned source. / Run the short training test with its small default settings. / Save the output and evaluate it before adapting the script to your dataset.
success: The validation training completes and its output can be loaded.
attention: CUDA and Triton version mismatches can prevent compilation. A successful short test does not qualify a much larger batch or context; check memory before scaling.

purpose: Use a local coding model from VS Code and Continue.
steps: Prepare and test an Ollama model that fits your node. / Install VS Code and Continue on the intended computer. / Configure Continue with the chosen local model endpoint. / Try an explanation and a small edit, then inspect the diff and run project checks.
success: Continue uses the intended endpoint and the small edit passes verification.
attention: The guide's 120B example needs substantial memory. Opening Ollama beyond localhost changes who can reach it; review that separately and use a controlled connection.

purpose: Read a Windows workflow for controlled image-to-video generation.
steps: Confirm the Windows RTX hardware and required applications. / Build the scene and generate matching first and last frames. / Run the ComfyUI video workflow with those frames. / Inspect the video before the optional upscaling step and preserve the project assets.
success: The generated video follows the intended scene and can be saved.
attention: This is a Windows GeForce/RTX PRO workflow, not a DGX Spark procedure. The separate ComfyUI Spark guide is the appropriate starting point for this cluster.

purpose: Read the desktop ComfyUI image and video introduction.
steps: Confirm the supported RTX desktop platform. / Install ComfyUI and run its starter image template. / Try the FLUX image path before the larger LTX video path. / Save generated outputs and reduce resolution if the chosen GPU runs out of memory.
success: The desktop workflow produces an image and an optional video.
attention: The current hardware table targets GeForce and RTX PRO, not DGX Spark. Use the Spark ComfyUI guide for Linux ARM64 setup.

purpose: Load a language model on one Spark and use it from your Mac.
steps: In Models, choose a model and download its files to the selected node. / On Load, review the recipe, image, memory share, context and endpoint protection. / Start through the normal confirmation and follow Tasks until the endpoint is ready. / Open Chat, send a short question, and use Unload when you want to free the node.
success: The correct model answers in Chat and Unload removes only its SparkBox-owned work.
attention: The source includes NVIDIA Sync and manual scripts; use SparkBox's own Load path for SparkBox-owned services. New upstream recipes still need compatibility review and live acceptance.

purpose: Understand and prepare a vLLM model spread across Sparks.
steps: Use Fabric and Topology to verify the actual links and participating nodes. / Make sure each node has a verified copy of the model and matching image. / In Models Load, review the supported recipe, parallel split and memory on every node. / Start only after preflight passes, test the endpoint, and unload the whole deployment through SparkBox.
success: All participating workers become ready and one endpoint answers correctly before a controlled unload.
attention: NVIDIA's current command-line examples cover two Sparks; three/four-node support in its overview is not proof for every recipe. SparkBox's four-node serving still needs its separate live acceptance.

purpose: Train a vision-language model on images or video.
steps: Prepare the playbook's local Docker build and selected dataset. / Start with the image path and verify base-model inference first. / Run a short LoRA training and compare the base and trained models in the UI. / Preserve the checkpoint before trying the longer video-training path.
success: The saved checkpoint loads and evaluation shows the intended change on held-out images or video.
attention: Video training can take a day or more. Keep datasets and outputs outside disposable containers, and evaluate false positives and missed events before relying on predictions.

purpose: Edit and run code on a Spark using VS Code.
steps: Choose local desktop or remote development before installing anything. / For local use, confirm ARM64 and follow the Linux ARM64 package path. / For remote use, configure the intended SSH connection in VS Code or NVIDIA Sync. / Open a small project on the node, edit a file and run it to verify the location.
success: VS Code identifies the intended remote or local environment and runs the test file there.
attention: Installing the local package changes the node. Keep SSH credentials in protected application settings; do not replace SparkBox's trusted identity record with a generic example.

purpose: Search and summarize sample video with NVIDIA's VSS stack.
steps: Check the DGX OS, driver, disk and model prerequisites. / Review the VSS deployment options and choose the documented Spark hybrid path. / Configure registry access and the remote model endpoints in their protected fields. / Process a short sample video and compare the summary and alerts with the actual footage.
success: The sample finishes and its indexed events, summary and timestamps can be inspected.
attention: This guide uses a local vision model and remote language models. Video-derived text may leave the node. Its cache-cleaner and network changes are not automatic; preserve SparkBox workloads and never bypass the protected-update checkpoint.
